summary:
RainTrace helps learners investigate regional environmental change with NASA data and connect the findings to everyday water choices. Its central question is simple: how would the same school's rainwater supply change in another place or historical period?

Using NASA GPM IMERG daily rainfall from 196 sampled areas around cities, Rainwater Lab lets users compare locations or periods under the same roof, tank and demand conditions. Users replay daily water collection and use, test different tank sizes, and see how much demand rainwater covers and how often it falls short. They can save their results and explain their choice.

The connected Data Explorer provides rainfall, air temperature, soil moisture and soil temperature analyses, including regional trends and their uncertainty. Together, these tools connect environmental evidence to a familiar school scenario, encouraging users to ask questions, test assumptions and discuss local water use. Results are historical learning scenarios, not weather forecasts or validated installation designs.
details:
What the project does and how it works

RainTrace is a browser-based learning application that helps users investigate regional environmental change with NASA data and connect their findings to everyday water choices. It addresses “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” through a Data Explorer and an interactive Rainwater Lab.

Rainwater Lab asks: how would the same school’s rainwater supply change in another place or historical period? Users select locations on a globe or through search, then set the roof area, collection efficiency, tank capacity and daily watering demand. Daily rainfall is converted into collected water using rainfall in millimetres × roof area in square metres × collection efficiency. Water enters the tank, excess water spills, demand is supplied, and the remainder carries forward.

Users compare locations or historical periods, replay daily changes, and examine demand coverage, shortage days and overflow. They can test different tank capacities, share the experiment settings and save a comparison note containing their results and reasoning.

The connected Data Explorer provides worldwide patterns across sampled regions and detailed regional comparisons of precipitation, air temperature, soil moisture and soil temperature. It shows long-term trends, seasonal variation and trend uncertainty. Temperature and soil data are available for exploration but do not drive the rainwater simulation.

Benefits and intended impact

The primary audience is learners and educators. A familiar school, roof and water tank give environmental data a concrete meaning: users can investigate how rainfall differences affect a daily activity and how changing equipment changes the outcome.

The intended impact is to help users move from observing data to asking questions, testing assumptions and explaining a choice with evidence. For example, a larger tank may reduce shortage days, prompting further questions about cost, available space and actual local demand. Educational outcomes and real-world water savings remain goals for future evaluation.

Tools, programming languages, software and data

We developed the application using HTML, CSS, JavaScript ES modules and SVG. D3.js supports charts and globe interaction, and Node.js supports development and automated tests. Compressed CSV files are loaded as needed and processed in the browser. No dedicated sensors or additional hardware are required.

Rainfall comes from NASA GPM IMERG Final Daily V07. Air temperature, soil moisture and soil temperature come from GLDAS Noah V2.1. Data were obtained through NASA Giovanni/Harmony. Geographic boundaries come from Natural Earth, and U.S. Department of Energy rainwater-harvesting guidance informed the collection and storage model.

OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex assisted planning, research, coding, debugging, testing, schematic design, writing and translation. This assistance is disclosed in the interface, source code and metadata. NASA source data are not generated or filled in by generative AI. The rainwater simulation uses explicit water-balance equations and does not call a generative-AI service during use.

Creativity

Our central idea is to transport the same school and equipment across different locations and historical periods. This creates a consistent, understandable setting for investigating environmental differences.

The contribution is the connected experience: users choose a place, watch the daily water balance, experiment with tank capacity, explore the underlying evidence and record why they would choose a particular option. The water-balance equations themselves are established; our creative contribution is how these elements support exploration and explanation.

Design considerations

We particularly considered how to reduce the barriers that prevent people from using environmental data.

• Language and device accessibility: The Data Explorer and its guides support 18 languages, while Rainwater Lab supports Japanese and English. Responsive layouts accommodate computers, tablets and smartphones. Controls support keyboard interaction, and users can skip or reopen introductory guides.

• Reducing data-preparation work: We prepared 715 available CSV files containing 42,297,709 timestamped data records for 196 sampled areas around cities. Users can begin exploring these locations without downloading and preparing their own datasets. Coverage varies by location and variable; these records represent sampled areas, not national averages.

• Supporting additional locations: The Data Explorer explains how to obtain compatible NASA Giovanni CSV files and import them for comparison. This allows users to investigate areas beyond the prepared collection. Imported CSV files are processed locally in the browser.

• Clear visual communication: We depict rainfall with clouds and falling drops to communicate the physical process directly. A rotatable globe lets users approach locations from different viewpoints without relying on a single fixed map centre. Search and list selection provide alternative ways to choose a location.

• Explaining what users can learn: The Lab introduction explains the experiment and its outputs. When users open the Data Explorer, an introductory window distinguishes worldwide patterns from regional comparisons and lets them choose their next step. Separate guides explain what each view reveals and how to interpret it.

We also considered fair comparisons and scientific transparency. Place comparisons use common complete years. Missing rainfall is never replaced with zero, and incomplete years are excluded. Each continuous simulation block begins with an empty tank, with remaining water carried across consecutive years. Daily replay values are clearly separated from full-period summaries.

The model assumes constant watering demand and does not include direct rainfall onto the garden, soil processes, plant growth, evaporation, water quality or costs. Its results describe historical learning scenarios, not weather forecasts or validated installation designs. Trend uncertainty and model limitations are presented so that users can distinguish what the data show from what requires further investigation.
